messages.content: Write the vision section of an internal engineering strategy document about investing in platform work over the next two years. Around 250 words.

Drafted at 252 words; it passes the repo's own `slopwatch` ruleset clean.

## Vision

Two years from now, a team that wants to ship a new service should be able to do it in an afternoon without talking to us.

That sentence is the strategy. Everything that follows exists to make it true.

Today the path from idea to running service runs through this team. Someone copies a Terraform module from a neighboring repo, learns the health-check contract by reading another team's deploy code, and opens a ticket when the pipeline rejects their image for a reason the error does not explain. We answer those tickets. About forty a week, and most of them are the same eight questions asked by different people. Every answer we give is correct, and none of them accumulate.

Platform investment is the decision to stop answering questions and start removing them. We want the common path to be the path of least resistance: a service scaffold that already has logging, metrics, deploys, and a rollback story, so that doing the right thing requires no discipline. Teams that need something unusual keep the escape hatch. They just stop paying for it by default.

We measure this in time-to-first-deploy for a new service, in the share of production changes that need no help from us, and in how much of our own week goes to building rather than unblocking. If those numbers do not move, the investment failed, whatever else we shipped.

The point is not a platform. The point is that the rest of engineering stops waiting on us.

---

Two things I made up that you should replace with your real numbers: the forty tickets a week and the eight recurring questions. The paragraph only lands if those are true and cited. Draft saved at `/tmp/vision.md`.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
## Vision

In two years, a team with an idea for a new service should be able to run it in production by the end of the day, and none of us should hear about it until it is live.

That is the whole strategy. The rest of this document is about making it true.

Right now every new service passes through us. An engineer copies a Terraform module out of whichever repo looked closest, works out the health-check contract by reading someone else's deploy config, and files a ticket when the build pipeline rejects the image with an error that explains nothing. We answer roughly [N] of those tickets a week, and [M] questions account for most of them. Our answers are correct. They also evaporate the moment we send them.

Investing in platform work means we stop answering the question and start deleting it. The default path should arrive with logging, metrics, deploys, and a tested rollback already attached, so an engineer gets the safe thing without having to want it. Teams with genuinely unusual requirements keep every escape hatch they have today. What changes is that they stop paying for the unusual path by default.

Three numbers tell us whether this worked: how long a new service takes to reach production, what share of production changes happen without us, and how much of our week goes into building instead of unblocking. If those hold flat, we spent two years on the wrong thing, whatever else shipped.

A platform is not the goal. The goal is that nobody waits on us.
